items.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

ctx.x: Well I’ve always wondered, who are those people that do those little things. But your relationship with radio — I saw a quote from you it said, “if you ask me about jazz radio I’m going to make a lot of enemies.” Do you remember that?

You know I don’t remember everything that I say because a lot of it’s not worth remembering and I’m just on a constant babble. But what happened was I went on the radio when I was 19, I was a junior in college when jazz radio was pretty much on FM and it was like a new phenomenon in the late fifties through, you know, the late sixties. FM radio, nobody listened to it. It was usually the AM station simulcast or there would be a classical station every once in a while. When the jazz stations started to catch on in…

serious kinds of music, jazz was one of them. It was a golden age so it was cool to dig Miles or cool to dig Brubeck or cool to dig whatever it was cool to dig. So jazz radio caught on. And it was basically a bunch of guys that dug jazz, some of whom were radio announcers, some of whom weren’t. Mostly back then the guys knew how to, you know, all jazz disc jockeys, you know had deep voices and were cool. We all spoke slowly and, you know, like that stuff. But we all loved the music and we kind of knew it. So it…
